Build & Tinker / MAKE · LEARN · DISCOVER

Build a paper bridge.

One sheet. A surprisingly strong idea.

Ages 6–1230 minIndoors

Can you make a sheet of paper hold more weight without adding another sheet? Build a small bridge between two stacks of books and compare a flat deck with a folded one.

Let's get started ↓Get the activity sheet
BEFORE YOU BEGIN

Gather your bits.

Tick things off as you get ready.

A note for grown-ups

Build on the floor or a low stable surface, away from feet. Use light, large blocks and low book stacks. This is a model only: never stand or lean on it. An adult should supervise setup and testing.

A little more guidance ↗
ONE STEP AT A TIME

Let's make it happen.

  1. Set up the gap

    Place two low stacks of books 15 cm apart. Lay one sheet across them so it rests equally on both sides. Keep the paper orientation the same for both tests.

  2. Predict and test the flat bridge

    Predict how many blocks it will hold. Add one block at a time gently at the centre. Stop when the paper bends into the gap. Record the last number it held before collapsing; zero is a useful result.

  3. Fold a new design

    Take the second sheet. Make accordion folds about 2 cm wide, with each long fold running from one book stack toward the other. The ridges should span the gap.

  4. Repeat the same test

    Use the same gap, blocks and loading spot. Add one block at a time and record the result. Stop if the stacks move or the blocks become unstable.

  5. Improve and explain

    Try a different fold width using another sheet if available. Sketch what you changed. Describe the result using your counts, including designs that did not improve.

THE LITTLE BIT OF LEARNING

What's happening here?

Folding changes the shape of the paper's cross-section. Ridges running across the gap can resist bending better than a flat sheet. The result also depends on the paper, fold shape and where you place the load.

Keep the wondering going.

  • What did you keep the same to make the comparison fair?
  • Where did each bridge start to bend?
  • Would turning the folds across the other direction change the result?

Make it work for you.

Keep it simple

Fold the paper together. Focus on comparing flat and folded, then count the blocks aloud.

Take it further

Repeat each design three times with fresh paper. Compare the results and explain why the numbers might vary.

Not quite going to plan?

Bridge slips off? Make the gap smaller for both designs and restart the comparison. Folds flattening? Sharpen the creases and check that the ridges run from support to support.
